| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | proc2_formality_choice | 1 | proc2_formality_choice_1 | formality | choose | single_choice | Y | N | none | 0 | Which sentence would be most suitable for a formal letter to the headteacher? | I just wanted to ask if we could maybe have extra chairs.; Can we get a couple more chairs for the hall?; I am writing to request two extra chairs for the hall.; We really need some more chairs for the hall, please. |  |  | Formal writing avoids chatty wording and uses more precise vocabulary.; The formal sentence uses precise vocabulary and avoids chatty phrasing.; The correct answer is: I am writing to request two extra chairs for the hall. |  | proc2_formality_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | proc2_formality_choice | 2 | proc2_formality_choice_2 | formality | choose | single_choice | Y | N | none | 0 | Which sentence sounds most formal? | The club got set up last year.; Last year was when the club got going.; The club was established last year.; The club was started up last year, really. |  |  | Formal writing avoids chatty wording and uses more precise vocabulary.; Formal register avoids casual expressions such as ‘got set up’.; The correct answer is: The club was established last year. |  | proc2_formality_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | proc2_formality_choice | 3 | proc2_formality_choice_3 | formality | choose | single_choice | Y | N | none | 0 | Choose the sentence that best fits a formal report. | A few pupils were off for the visit.; Quite a few pupils were missing from it.; Several pupils were absent from the visit.; Some pupils didn't come on the trip. |  |  | Formal writing avoids chatty wording and uses more precise vocabulary.; Formal writing often chooses more precise vocabulary and sentence structure.; The correct answer is: Several pupils were absent from the visit. |  | proc2_formality_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | proc2_formality_choice | 4 | proc2_formality_choice_4 | formality | choose | single_choice | Y | N | none | 0 | Which sentence is most appropriate for a school newsletter? | We're so excited about the new library opening!; The new library is opening and it's going to be great.; We are delighted to announce the opening of the new library.; Guess what – there's a new library starting up. |  |  | Formal writing avoids chatty wording and uses more precise vocabulary.; Formal register uses measured language rather than informal exclamations.; The correct answer is: We are delighted to announce the opening of the new library. |  | proc2_formality_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | proc2_formality_choice | 5 | proc2_formality_choice_5 | formality | choose | single_choice | Y | N | none | 0 | Choose the sentence that fits best in a formal invitation. | Can everyone turn up by half six?; Guests are kindly requested to arrive by half past six.; Everyone should come at like half six.; Please try to get there by about six-thirty. |  |  | Formal writing avoids chatty wording and uses more precise vocabulary.; Formal invitations use passive or impersonal constructions and precise time references.; The correct answer is: Guests are kindly requested to arrive by half past six. |  | proc2_formality_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | proc2_formality_choice | 6 | proc2_formality_choice_6 | formality | choose | single_choice | Y | N | none | 0 | Which sentence would be most suitable for a formal science report? | We tried the experiment and it sort of worked.; We just did the experiment and it worked out fine.; The experiment was conducted under controlled conditions.; The experiment happened and everything was OK. |  |  | Formal writing avoids chatty wording and uses more precise vocabulary.; Formal scientific writing uses passive constructions and precise vocabulary.; The correct answer is: The experiment was conducted under controlled conditions. |  | proc2_formality_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | proc2_formality_choice | 7 | proc2_formality_choice_7 | formality | choose | single_choice | Y | N | none | 0 | Which sentence is most appropriate for an official complaint letter? | Your service was awful and I'm not happy about it.; I want to tell you the service was rubbish.; Just so you know, the service was really bad.; I wish to draw your attention to the unsatisfactory service we received. |  |  | Formal writing avoids chatty wording and uses more precise vocabulary.; Formal complaint letters use measured, impersonal language rather than emotional outbursts.; The correct answer is: I wish to draw your attention to the unsatisfactory service we received. |  | proc2_formality_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | proc2_formality_choice | 8 | proc2_formality_choice_8 | formality | choose | single_choice | Y | N | none | 0 | Which sentence fits best in a formal assembly speech? | Here's the person who's going to talk to us now.; So yeah, this is the speaker we got in today.; I'm dead chuffed to get our speaker up here.; It is with great pleasure that I introduce our guest speaker. |  |  | Formal writing avoids chatty wording and uses more precise vocabulary.; Formal spoken register avoids slang and uses established ceremonial phrases.; The correct answer is: It is with great pleasure that I introduce our guest speaker. |  | proc2_formality_choice | draft_only |

| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_active_passive_choice | 1 | qg_active_passive_choice_1 | active_passive | choose | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Which sentence is written in the passive voice? | Before assembly, the caretaker locked the hall.; The caretaker locked the hall before assembly.; The hall was locked by the caretaker before assembly.; The caretaker was locking the hall before assembly. | The hall was locked by the caretaker before assembly. | active_passive_confusion | In passive voice, the thing affected often comes before the doer.; The hall receives the action, so it comes first in the passive sentence.; The passive sentence is: The hall was locked by the caretaker before assembly. |  | qg_active_passive_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_active_passive_choice | 2 | qg_active_passive_choice_2 | active_passive | choose | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Which sentence is written in the passive voice? | Aisha painted the scenery for the play.; For the play, Aisha painted the scenery.; The scenery was painted by Aisha for the play.; Aisha was painting the scenery for the play. | The scenery was painted by Aisha for the play. | active_passive_confusion | In passive voice, the thing affected often comes before the doer.; The passive voice focuses on the scenery rather than the person doing the painting.; The passive sentence is: The scenery was painted by Aisha for the play. |  | qg_active_passive_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_active_passive_choice | 3 | qg_active_passive_choice_3 | active_passive | choose | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Which sentence is written in the passive voice? | The gardener trimmed the hedges on Monday.; On Monday, the gardener trimmed the hedges.; The hedges were trimmed by the gardener on Monday.; The gardener was trimming the hedges on Monday. | The hedges were trimmed by the gardener on Monday. | active_passive_confusion | In passive voice, the thing affected often comes before the doer.; The hedges receive the action and come first in the passive sentence.; The passive sentence is: The hedges were trimmed by the gardener on Monday. |  | qg_active_passive_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_active_passive_choice | 4 | qg_active_passive_choice_4 | active_passive | choose | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Which sentence is written in the passive voice? | Noah carried the boxes to the office.; Noah was carrying the boxes to the office.; The boxes were carried by Noah to the office.; To the office, Noah carried the boxes. | The boxes were carried by Noah to the office. | active_passive_confusion | In passive voice, the thing affected often comes before the doer.; In the passive, the boxes are placed before the doer.; The passive sentence is: The boxes were carried by Noah to the office. |  | qg_active_passive_choice | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_active_passive_choice | 5 | qg_active_passive_choice_5 | active_passive | choose | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Which sentence is written in the passive voice? | The chef prepared the meal before noon.; The meal was prepared by the chef before noon.; Before noon, the chef prepared the meal.; The chef was preparing the meal before noon. | The meal was prepared by the chef before noon. | active_passive_confusion | In passive voice, the thing affected often comes before the doer.; The passive puts the thing affected (the meal) into the subject position.; The passive sentence is: The meal was prepared by the chef before noon. |  | qg_active_passive_choice | draft_only |

| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_hyphen_ambiguity_explain | 1 | qg_hyphen_ambiguity_explain_1 | hyphen_ambiguity | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why does the hyphen matter in small-animal hospital rather than small animal hospital? | The hyphen shows a missing letter.; The hyphen shows that the hospital building is small.; The hyphen shows that the hospital is for small animals.; The hyphen marks a fronted adverbial. | The hyphen shows that the hospital is for small animals. | hyphen_ambiguity_confusion | A hyphen can join words so they work as one describing idea before a noun.; The hyphen joins 'small' and 'animal' so they work together before 'hospital'. |  | qg_hyphen_ambiguity_explain | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_hyphen_ambiguity_explain | 2 | qg_hyphen_ambiguity_explain_2 | hyphen_ambiguity | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why does the hyphen matter in last-minute poster rather than last minute poster? | The hyphen shows that the poster is the final minute.; The hyphen marks direct speech.; The hyphen shows that 'last-minute' is one describing idea before 'poster'.; The hyphen joins two complete clauses. | The hyphen shows that 'last-minute' is one describing idea before 'poster'. | hyphen_ambiguity_confusion | A hyphen can join words so they work as one describing idea before a noun.; The compound adjective comes before the noun, so the hyphen protects the intended meaning. |  | qg_hyphen_ambiguity_explain | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_hyphen_ambiguity_explain | 3 | qg_hyphen_ambiguity_explain_3 | hyphen_ambiguity | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why does the hyphen matter in well-known author rather than well known author? | The hyphen shows the author owns a well.; The hyphen separates two independent clauses.; The hyphen shows that 'well-known' is one describing idea before 'author'.; The hyphen turns well into a noun. | The hyphen shows that 'well-known' is one describing idea before 'author'. | hyphen_ambiguity_confusion | A hyphen can join words so they work as one describing idea before a noun.; Compound adjectives before a noun use a hyphen to show they form a single modifier. |  | qg_hyphen_ambiguity_explain | draft_only |

| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p3_sentence_functions_explain | 1 | qg_p3_sentence_functions_explain_1 | sentence_functions | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why is this sentence a question?Where did the caretaker leave the keys? | It is a grammatical exclamation because it ends with a question mark.; It tells the caretaker to leave the keys somewhere.; It asks for information directly, so it is a question.; It gives information about where the keys are. | It asks for information directly, so it is a question. | sentence_function_confusion | Choose the option that explains the grammar relationship.; A question asks something directly; the question mark supports that function.; The best explanation is: It asks for information directly, so it is a question. |  | qg_p3_sentence_functions_explain | draft_only |

| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p3_noun_phrases_explain | 28 | qg_p3_noun_phrases_explain_28 | noun_phrases | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why is this an expanded noun phrase rather than a clause?the lighthouse on the cliff | It has no verb; it is a noun phrase centred on lighthouse.; It is a sentence because it begins with the.; It is a clause because cliff is a subject.; It is a clause because every phrase with on has a verb. | It has no verb; it is a noun phrase centred on lighthouse. | noun_phrase_confusion | Choose the option that explains the grammar relationship.; A clause normally has a verb; this group names and expands a noun.; The best explanation is: It has no verb; it is a noun phrase centred on lighthouse. |  | qg_p3_noun_phrases_explain | draft_only |

| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p3_active_passive_explain | 20 | qg_p3_active_passive_explain_20 | active_passive | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why does this passive sentence keep the meaning of the active one?The scenery was painted by Aisha. | Aisha is still the doer, but the scenery has been moved to the subject position.; The tense changes from past to future.; The scenery becomes the person doing the painting.; The sentence becomes a question about Aisha. | Aisha is still the doer, but the scenery has been moved to the subject position. | active_passive_confusion | Choose the option that explains the grammar relationship.; Active and passive can keep the same basic event while changing emphasis.; The best explanation is: Aisha is still the doer, but the scenery has been moved to the subject position. |  | qg_p3_active_passive_explain | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p3_active_passive_explain | 21 | qg_p3_active_passive_explain_21 | active_passive | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why is this passive sentence missing the doer?The medals were presented after assembly. | The sentence is active because no by-phrase appears.; Passive voice can leave out the by-phrase when the doer is unknown or less important.; The sentence is informal because the doer is hidden.; The medals must be the doers because they come first. | Passive voice can leave out the by-phrase when the doer is unknown or less important. | active_passive_confusion | Choose the option that explains the grammar relationship.; A passive sentence does not have to include the doer.; The best explanation is: Passive voice can leave out the by-phrase when the doer is unknown or less important. |  | qg_p3_active_passive_explain | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p3_active_passive_explain | 22 | qg_p3_active_passive_explain_22 | active_passive | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why is this sentence active even though the subject is not a person?The storm destroyed the fence. | Only people can be the subject in active voice.; It is passive because storms are natural forces.; The storm is the subject that does the action of destroying.; It is passive because the fence receives the action. | The storm is the subject that does the action of destroying. | active_passive_confusion | Choose the option that explains the grammar relationship.; Any noun phrase that does the verb can be the subject in active voice, including non-human agents.; The best explanation is: The storm is the subject that does the action of destroying. |  | qg_p3_active_passive_explain | draft_only |

| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p3_subject_object_explain | 1 | qg_p3_subject_object_explain_1 | subject_object | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why is 'the soup' the object?The chef tasted the soup. | The soup is an adverbial because it tells when.; The soup does the action.; The soup receives the action of tasting.; The soup is the subject because it is at the end. | The soup receives the action of tasting. | subject_object_confusion | Choose the option that explains the grammar relationship.; The object is often the noun phrase that the action is done to.; The best explanation is: The soup receives the action of tasting. |  | qg_p3_subject_object_explain | draft_only |
| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p3_subject_object_explain | 2 | qg_p3_subject_object_explain_2 | subject_object | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why is 'Before lunch' not the subject?Before lunch, Aisha packed the kit. | Before lunch is the subject because it comes first.; Before lunch is the verb phrase.; Before lunch is an adverbial; Aisha does the action.; Before lunch is the object because it receives packing. | Before lunch is an adverbial; Aisha does the action. | subject_object_confusion | Choose the option that explains the grammar relationship.; A fronted adverbial can come first, but the subject is still who or what does the verb.; The best explanation is: Before lunch is an adverbial; Aisha does the action. |  | qg_p3_subject_object_explain | draft_only |

| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p3_subject_object_explain | 28 | qg_p3_subject_object_explain_28 | subject_object | explain | single_choice | Y | N | exact | 1 | Why is 'the trophy' the subject in this passive sentence?The trophy was lifted by Aisha. | The trophy is before the verb phrase and the sentence is about what happened to it.; By Aisha is the subject because it comes after by.; The trophy is the object because every affected thing is always the object.; Aisha must be the subject because she is the doer. | The trophy is before the verb phrase and the sentence is about what happened to it. | subject_object_confusion | Choose the option that explains the grammar relationship.; In passive voice, the grammatical subject can be the thing affected.; The best explanation is: The trophy is before the verb phrase and the sentence is about what happened to it. |  | qg_p3_subject_object_explain | draft_only |

| grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p4_sentence_speech_transfer | 1 | qg_p4_sentence_speech_transfer_1 | sentence_functions; speech_punctuation | choose | single_choice | Y | Y | exact | 1 | Which option correctly punctuates the direct speech AND keeps the whole sentence as a question?Did Mum really say ___ | Did Mum really say "Pack your bag now"?; Did Mum really say, "Pack your bag now"?; Did Mum really say, "Pack your bag now?" | Did Mum really say, "Pack your bag now"? | speech_punctuation_confusion | This question tests sentence functions and speech punctuation together.; The whole sentence is a question (sentence function), so the question mark comes outside the closing speech marks. | grammar-qg-p14-2026-05-01 | qg_p4_possession_hyphen_clarity_transfer | 1 | qg_p4_possession_hyphen_clarity_transfer_1 | apostrophes_possession; hyphen_ambiguity | choose | single_choice | Y | Y | exact | 1 | Which option correctly uses both the possessive apostrophe AND a hyphen to avoid ambiguity?The well known author's latest book topped the charts. | The well-known authors' latest book topped the charts.; The well known authors latest book topped the charts.; The well-known author's latest book topped the charts.; The well known author's latest book topped the charts. | The well-known author's latest book topped the charts. | hyphen_ambiguity_confusion | This question tests apostrophes possession and hyphen ambiguity together.; A hyphen in 'well-known' links the compound adjective before the noun, avoiding the misreading 'well known-author'.
